t: Find Maximum Non-decreasing Array Length — DP on Segment Sums with a Monotonic Stack
o:
We may repeatedly replace any contiguous subarray by its sum, and we want the longest possible non-decreasing result. Any final array corresponds to a partition of `nums` into consecutive segments (each segment collapsed to its sum), such that the segment sums are non-decreasing. So the task is: **partition the array into the maximum number of contiguous pieces whose sums form a non-decreasing sequence**.

In example 1 `[5,2,2]`, every 2-piece partition (`[5|2,2] -> [5,4]`, `[5,2|2] -> [7,2]`) fails, so the answer is the single piece `[9]`. In example 2 the array already works as four pieces. In example 3 `[4,3,2,6]` we merge `[3,2]` into `5`, giving pieces `4 | 5 | 6`.

With `n` up to 1e5 we need roughly linear time, which rules out trying all partitions. Prefix sums plus a DP over cut positions, accelerated so each position is resolved quickly, is the intended path.
k: The answer equals the maximum number of segments in a partition of nums whose segment sums are non-decreasing.
For each cut point store the best length achievable and, among those, the smallest possible last-segment sum — a smaller last sum never hurts future extensions.
A candidate cut j is usable for position i iff prefix[i] >= prefix[j] + last[j]; keeping candidates sorted by that key lets us binary-search the best j in O(log n).
Dominated candidates (length not larger and key not smaller) can be popped from a stack, keeping the structure clean.

a.n: Approach 1: Quadratic DP over cut points
a.i: Let `len[i]` be the maximum number of segments for prefix `0..i-1` and `last[i]` the minimal possible last-segment sum achieving it. To end a segment at `i`, pick a previous cut `j`: the new segment sums to `pre[i]-pre[j]` and must be at least `last[j]`. Among all valid `j` we prefer maximal `len[j]`, breaking ties by minimal resulting `last`. Trying every `j` for every `i` gives an $O(n^2)$ baseline that clarifies the recurrence before we optimize it.
s: Build prefix sums pre where pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements.
For each i from 1..n, scan all j<i with pre[i]-pre[j] >= last[j].
Take the j maximizing len[j], tie-broken by minimal pre[i]-pre[j]; set len[i]=len[j]+1, last[i]=that difference.
If no valid j exists, fall back to merging the whole prefix: len[i]=1, last[i]=pre[i]. Answer is len[n].
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n positions we scan all previous cut points.
a.sp: O(n) — prefix sums plus the DP arrays.

a.n: Approach 2: Monotonic stack of candidates + binary search (optimal)
a.i: Rewrite the validity condition `pre[i] - pre[j] >= last[j]` as `pre[i] >= pre[j] + last[j]`. Define `key[j] = pre[j] + last[j]`. We keep a stack of candidate cut points whose keys are strictly increasing and whose lengths are non-decreasing; then for each `i` the best predecessor is simply the **rightmost** candidate with `key <= pre[i]` (it has maximal length and, being latest, maximizes `pre[j]`, minimizing the new last sum), found by binary search. Before pushing `i`, pop any top that is dominated: length `<= len[i]` and key `>= key[i]`. Each index is pushed and popped once, giving near-linear time.
s: Maintain a stack of triples (key, len, index) with strictly increasing keys and non-decreasing lengths.
For each i, binary search the rightmost stack entry with key <= pre[i].
Set len[i] = entry.len + 1 and last[i] = pre[i] - entry.index-prefix; if none qualifies, use len[i] = 1, last[i] = pre[i].
Pop stack tops with len <= len[i] and key >= pre[i] + last[i], then push i; return the length stored for n.
a.t: O(n log n) — each index is pushed/popped at most once, and each step does one O(log n) binary search over the stack.
a.sp: O(n) — prefix sums and the candidate stack.

w: In an interview, start from the partition reformulation and the quadratic DP to nail the recurrence, then present the monotonic-stack + binary-search version as the optimal answer. Common pitfalls: forgetting the fallback `len=1, last=prefix` when no predecessor qualifies (merging everything is always legal); using 32-bit integers — sums reach 1e10, so use 64-bit in C++/Java; picking the wrong tie-break (among equally long predecessors choose the latest index to minimize the new last sum); and off-by-one issues between prefix indices and cut positions. Edge cases: strictly decreasing arrays (answer 1), already sorted arrays (answer n), and single-element arrays (answer 1). Likely follow-ups: reconstructing an actual optimal partition (store parent pointers), or handling zeros/negatives, which would break the monotonicity assumptions and require a different technique.
